result.markdown: --- title: "Federated OMOP analysis with dsOMOP" subtitle: "A hands-on tutorial — exploring real hospital data across three sites, without the data ever leaving them" format: html execute: warning: false message: false error: true --- Download the R script (.R) Source (.Rmd) # Welcome In this tutorial you will analyse **real-world hospital data** that lives in **three different hospitals at once** — and you will do it **without ever seeing or downloading a single patient's record**. - **OMOP CDM** is a standard *shape* for health data: every hospital stores patients, diagnoses, drugs and labs in the same tables (`person`, `condition_occurrence`, `drug_exposure`, `measurement`, ...). - **DataSHIELD** is the safety layer: you send *commands*, each hospital runs them on its own data and returns **only aggregated, non-disclosive results**. - **dsOMOP** is the bridge that lets DataSHIELD speak OMOP. ::: {.callout-important} ## The golden rule You never hold patient-level data on your laptop. Every result is checked by a **disclosure filter** on each server before it is returned. If a result would describe too few people, the server hides it. ::: We work with **MIMIC** (an intensive-care database, ~100 patients here): connect → explore → learn the **recipe** for building analysis tables → filter → and finish with a real **regression model**. # 1. Connecting to the federation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(DSI) library(DSOpal) library(dsBaseClient) library(dsOMOPClient) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} builder <- DSI::newDSLoginBuilder() builder$append(server = "nairobi", url = "https://nairobi.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") builder$append(server = "douala", url = "https://douala.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") builder$append(server = "dakar", url = "https://dakar.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") conns <- DSI::datashield.login(logins = builder$build()) ds.omop.connect(resource = "omop_demo.mimic", symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} Forgetting `profile = "omop"` is the #1 beginner mistake — without it the `ds.omop.*` functions aren't available. ::: # 2. Reading the map: tables and columns The clinical (`CDM`) tables (consistent across the three sites, so one view represents the federation): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tabs <- ds.omop.tables(symbol = "omop", conns = conns)[[1]] tabs[tabs$schema_category == "CDM", c("table_name", "has_person_id")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> table_name has_person_id #> 1 person TRUE #> 2 observation_period TRUE #> 3 visit_occurrence TRUE #> 4 visit_detail TRUE #> 5 condition_occurrence TRUE #> 6 drug_exposure TRUE #> 7 procedure_occurrence TRUE #> 8 device_exposure TRUE #> 9 measurement TRUE #> 10 observation TRUE #> 11 death TRUE #> 12 note TRUE #> 13 note_nlp FALSE #> 14 specimen TRUE #> 15 fact_relationship FALSE #> 18 location FALSE #> 19 care_site FALSE #> 20 provider FALSE #> 21 payer_plan_period TRUE #> 22 cost FALSE #> 23 condition_era TRUE #> 24 drug_era TRUE #> 25 dose_era TRUE #> 26 cdm_source FALSE #> 27 metadata FALSE #> achilles_performance achilles_performance FALSE #> attribute_definition attribute_definition FALSE ``` ::: ::: The columns of the `measurement` table (where labs and vital signs live): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.columns("measurement", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)[[1]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> column_name cdm_datatype db_datatype #> 1 measurement_id integer bigint #> 2 person_id integer bigint #> 3 measurement_concept_id integer bigint #> 4 measurement_date date date #> 5 measurement_datetime datetime timestamp without time zone #> 6 measurement_time varchar(10) text #> 7 measurement_type_concept_id integer bigint #> 8 operator_concept_id integer bigint #> 9 value_as_number float numeric #> 10 value_as_concept_id integer bigint #> 11 unit_concept_id integer bigint #> 12 range_low float numeric #> 13 range_high float numeric #> 14 provider_id integer bigint #> 15 visit_occurrence_id integer bigint #> 16 visit_detail_id integer bigint #> 17 measurement_source_value varchar(50) text #> 18 measurement_source_concept_id integer bigint #> 19 unit_source_value varchar(50) text #> 20 value_source_value varchar(50) text #> concept_role fk_domain is_date is_sensitive is_blocked #> 1 non_concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 2 non_concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 3 domain_concept Measurement FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 4 non_concept TRUE FALSE FALSE #> 5 non_concept TRUE FALSE FALSE #> 6 non_concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 7 type_concept Type Concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 8 attribute_concept Meas Value Operator FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 9 non_concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 10 attribute_concept Meas Value FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 11 attribute_concept Unit FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 12 non_concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 13 non_concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 14 non_concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 15 non_concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 16 non_concept FALSE FALSE FALSE #> 17 non_concept FALSE TRUE TRUE #> 18 source_concept Measurement FALSE TRUE TRUE #> 19 non_concept FALSE TRUE TRUE #> 20 non_concept FALSE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ::: # 3. Who are these patients? Gender, **pooled** across the three sites: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.concept.prevalence("person", concept_col = "gender_concept_id", scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> concept_id n_persons concept_name #> 1 8507 55 MALE #> 2 8532 35 FEMALE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Concepts translate themselves You got `MALE` / `FEMALE`, not codes like `8507` / `8532` — any `*_concept_id` column is automatically translated. **Concept translation is on by default.** ::: And their **birth years** — `ds.omop.value.histogram()` draws a disclosure-safe, federation-wide histogram of any numeric column when you pass `plot = TRUE`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.value.histogram("person", value_col = "year_of_birth", nbins = 6, plot = TRUE, xlab = "Year of birth", main = "Patient birth years (pooled)", symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dsomop_files/figure-html/birth-hist-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} This extract was re-anchored so its records run through **2024**; subtract a birth year from 2024 for an age (earlier birth years = older patients). We'll get age directly from the recipe in Section 7. ::: # 4. Discovering what was recorded The most common diagnoses, **pooled** and ranked by distinct patients: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.concept.prevalence("condition_occurrence", metric = "persons", top_n = 10, scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> concept_id n_persons concept_name #> 1 4145513 85 ECG: sinus rhythm #> 2 4140598 60 ECG: sinus tachycardia #> 3 433753 55 Alcohol abuse #> 4 320128 45 Essential hypertension #> 5 432867 45 Hyperlipidemia ``` ::: ::: Don't know a concept's code? **Search** for it: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.concept.search("hyperlipidemia", domain = "Condition", limit = 5, symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> concept_id concept_name domain_id vocabulary_id standard_concept #> 1 432867 Hyperlipidemia Condition SNOMED S #> concept_class_id concept_code valid_start_date valid_end_date invalid_reason #> 1 Disorder 55822004 1970-01-01 2099-12-31 ``` ::: ::: And **look up** codes you already have: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.concept.lookup(c(320128, 432867, 3027018), symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> concept_id concept_name domain_id vocabulary_id standard_concept #> 1 320128 Essential hypertension Condition SNOMED S #> 2 432867 Hyperlipidemia Condition SNOMED S #> 3 3027018 Heart rate Measurement LOINC S ``` ::: ::: # 5. Numeric measurements: shape matters `ds.omop.column.stats()` returns a disclosure-safe summary (counts, mean, sd, a 5th–95th-percentile band — never the true min/max). Heart rate (`3027018`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.column.stats("measurement", "value_as_number", concept_id = 3027018, scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $n_total #> [1] 19315 #> #> $mean #> [1] 95.73897 #> #> $sd #> [1] 19.25911 ``` ::: ::: Its distribution — again with `plot = TRUE`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.value.histogram("measurement", value_col = "value_as_number", concept_id = 3027018, nbins = 7, plot = TRUE, xlab = "Heart rate (bpm)", main = "Heart rate (pooled across sites)", symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dsomop_files/figure-html/hr-hist-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Heart rate is **roughly symmetric**. Contrast it with **serum creatinine** (`3016723`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.value.histogram("measurement", value_col = "value_as_number", concept_id = 3016723, nbins = 9, plot = TRUE, col = "#C44E52", xlab = "Creatinine (mg/dL)", main = "Serum creatinine (pooled across sites)", symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dsomop_files/figure-html/creat-hist-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Symmetric vs skewed Creatinine has a **long right tail** (a minority with kidney injury) that pulls its mean above the median — so the mean overstates the "typical" patient. Always look at the shape before trusting a mean. ::: # 6. A categorical measurement: heart rhythm Some measurements store a *category* in `value_as_concept_id` instead of a number. Heart **rhythm** is the measurement concept `3022318`; its recorded answers live in `value_as_concept_id`. Count them, pooled: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.value.counts("measurement", "value_as_concept_id", concept_id = 3022318, scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> n concept_name value #> 1 6530 Sinus rhythm 45877096 #> 2 2400 Atrial fibrillation 45883018 #> 3 2300 Sinus tachycardia 45879290 #> 4 665 concept_0 0 #> 5 385 Sinus bradycardia 21499419 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## How to read this - The first argument (`"measurement"`) is the **table** we look in; `concept_id = 3022318` is the measurement; `value_as_concept_id` is the column we count. (For a social fact you'd look in `"observation"` instead.) - **`concept_name`** is each answer's translated label; **`value`** is its raw concept code (e.g. `45877096` = "Sinus rhythm"). - **`concept_0`** (value `0`) is OMOP's **unmapped** bucket — records whose value didn't map to a standard concept. It is *not* suppression and not a bug. ::: # 7. The recipe: building analysis tables To **model** anything we need one row per patient and one column per variable. You describe that table with a **recipe**; the servers build it for you. Every recipe has the same shape — here is the skeleton (don't run this; it's a template): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} omop_recipe( variables = list( # WHAT columns you want omop_variable(), # a person column, or something built from a concept_id omop_variable_age(), # the patient's age omop_variable() # ...add as many as you need ), filters = list(), # OPTIONAL: restrict the population (Section 8) output = omop_output() # the table SHAPE you want (usually wide = one row/patient) ) recipe_execute() # build it on each server into a named symbol ``` ::: ## 7.1 Start simple — sex and age ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec0 <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2024) ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide") ) recipe_execute(rec0, out = c(study = "M0"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: **Always inspect what the server built**, then look at each variable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.colnames("M0", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $nairobi #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" #> #> $douala #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" #> #> $dakar #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.dim("M0", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $`dimensions of M0 in nairobi` #> [1] 35 3 #> #> $`dimensions of M0 in douala` #> [1] 25 3 #> #> $`dimensions of M0 in dakar` #> [1] 40 3 #> #> $`dimensions of M0 in combined studies` #> [1] 100 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.table("M0$sex", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Data in all studies were valid #> #> Study 1 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 2 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 3 : No errors reported from this study ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> M0$sex #> F M NA #> 43 57 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.summary("M0$age", datasources = conns)[[1]][["quantiles & mean"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 5% 10% 25% 50% 75% 90% 95% Mean #> 38.90000 46.40000 52.00000 63.00000 76.50000 86.00000 88.90000 63.88571 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Why `year = 2024`? Age needs a reference year. This extract runs through 2024, so we anchor age there rather than to "today" (which would drift on every rebuild). The age **filter** in Section 8 takes the same `year =`. ::: ## 7.2 Grow it — numbers, flags and counts Mix the variable types we met: a categorical (`sex`), a numeric mean (`heart_rate`), two **binary** condition flags, and a **count** (`n_visits`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2024), omop_variable(table = "measurement", concept_id = 3027018, format = "mean", name = "heart_rate"), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 320128, format = "binary", name = "hypertension"), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 432867, format = "binary", name = "hyperlipidemia"), omop_variable(table = "visit_occurrence", format = "count", name = "n_visits") ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide") ) recipe_execute(rec, out = c(study = "M"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ds.colnames("M", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $nairobi #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" "hyperlipidemia" #> [5] "n_visits" "sex" "age" #> #> $douala #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" "hyperlipidemia" #> [5] "n_visits" "sex" "age" #> #> $dakar #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" "hyperlipidemia" #> [5] "n_visits" "sex" "age" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.dim("M", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $`dimensions of M in nairobi` #> [1] 35 7 #> #> $`dimensions of M in douala` #> [1] 25 7 #> #> $`dimensions of M in dakar` #> [1] 40 7 #> #> $`dimensions of M in combined studies` #> [1] 100 7 ``` ::: ::: **Look at every variable in its natural way.** Numeric columns → a quantile summary: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.summary("M$age", datasources = conns)[[1]][["quantiles & mean"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 5% 10% 25% 50% 75% 90% 95% Mean #> 38.90000 46.40000 52.00000 63.00000 76.50000 86.00000 88.90000 63.88571 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.summary("M$heart_rate", datasources = conns)[[1]][["quantiles & mean"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 5% 10% 25% 50% 75% 90% 95% Mean #> 68.85334 70.28388 78.92535 88.44355 98.68583 104.52308 107.79092 88.63992 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.summary("M$n_visits", datasources = conns)[[1]][["quantiles & mean"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 5% 10% 25% 50% 75% 90% 95% Mean #> 1.00000 1.00000 1.50000 3.00000 8.50000 29.80000 39.20000 10.54286 ``` ::: ::: Categorical / binary columns → a frequency table: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.table("M$sex", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Data in all studies were valid #> #> Study 1 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 2 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 3 : No errors reported from this study ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> M$sex #> F M NA #> 43 57 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.table("M$hypertension", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Data in all studies were valid #> #> Study 1 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 2 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 3 : No errors reported from this study ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> M$hypertension #> 0 1 NA #> 47 53 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.table("M$hyperlipidemia", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Data in all studies were valid #> #> Study 1 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 2 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 3 : No errors reported from this study ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> M$hyperlipidemia #> 0 1 NA #> 53 47 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## `binary` vs `count` `format = "binary"` is *does this patient have it at all?* (0/1). `format = "count"` is *how many records?* — here `n_visits` is right-skewed (most patients few visits, a handful many). ::: ## 7.3 One recipe, several tables A recipe can declare **several outputs**, each selecting a **different subset of variables**, so one extraction produces several purpose-built tables (e.g. a demographics table and a clinical one) — list them with `outputs = list(...)`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_multi <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2024), omop_variable(table = "measurement", concept_id = 3027018, format = "mean", name = "heart_rate"), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 320128, format = "binary", name = "hypertension") ), outputs = list( omop_output(name = "demographics", variables = c("sex", "age"), type = "wide"), omop_output(name = "clinical", variables = c("heart_rate", "hypertension"), type = "wide") ) ) recipe_execute(rec_multi, out = c(demographics = "DEMO", clinical = "CLIN"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ds.colnames("DEMO", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $nairobi #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" #> #> $douala #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" #> #> $dakar #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.colnames("CLIN", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $nairobi #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" #> #> $douala #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" #> #> $dakar #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" ``` ::: ::: # 8. Filtering at extraction Often you only want a **subpopulation**. Add a `filters` element so the servers only build the rows you ask for. Filters can only ever **shrink** a population, so they are safe. Here: **patients aged 50+ who have hyperlipidemia**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_sub <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2024) ), filters = list( older = omop_filter_age(min = 50, year = 2024), with_lipids = omop_filter_has_concept(concept_id = 432867, table = "condition_occurrence") ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide") ) recipe_execute(rec_sub, out = c(study = "SUB"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: The cohort is smaller, and the minimum age respects the 50+ floor: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.dim("SUB", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $`dimensions of SUB in nairobi` #> [1] 14 3 #> #> $`dimensions of SUB in douala` #> [1] 11 3 #> #> $`dimensions of SUB in dakar` #> [1] 19 3 #> #> $`dimensions of SUB in combined studies` #> [1] 44 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.summary("SUB$age", datasources = conns)[[1]][["quantiles & mean"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 5% 10% 25% 50% 75% 90% 95% Mean #> 54.55000 57.30000 60.75000 75.00000 84.50000 87.40000 89.75000 72.64286 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} The safe filter types all shrink a population: `omop_filter_sex()`, `omop_filter_age()` / age groups, `omop_filter_has_concept()`, and ranges. (You can also restrict by sex with `omop_filter_sex("F")`.) ::: # 9. A real model: what predicts a diagnosis? A logistic regression of **hyperlipidemia** on age and sex, fitted jointly across the three hospitals. We show the raw `ds.glm` coefficients (`P_OR` is the odds ratio, with its 95% CI in the `*.P_OR` columns): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit1 <- ds.glm(formula = "M$hyperlipidemia ~ M$age + M$sex", family = "binomial", datasources = conns) fit1$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Estimate Std. Error z-value p-value low0.95CI.LP #> (Intercept) -4.59371247 1.15761941 -3.96824071 7.240518e-05 -6.8626048 #> M$age 0.07020260 0.01719118 4.08364005 4.433569e-05 0.0365085 #> M$sexM -0.01449884 0.45779165 -0.03167126 9.747342e-01 -0.9117540 #> high0.95CI.LP P_OR low0.95CI.P_OR high0.95CI.P_OR #> (Intercept) -2.3248201 0.01001394 0.001045092 0.08908812 #> M$age 0.1038967 1.07272550 1.037183125 1.10948584 #> M$sexM 0.8827563 0.98560576 0.401818820 2.41755406 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Reading it **age** is a clear, **significant** predictor (`P_OR` > 1, tiny `p-value`); **sex** is not (`P_OR` ≈ 1). One clear effect, one null — produced without touching a patient record. ::: A **multivariable** model — hypertension on age, sex and hyperlipidemia: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit2 <- ds.glm(formula = "M$hypertension ~ M$age + M$sex + M$hyperlipidemia", family = "binomial", datasources = conns) fit2$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Estimate Std. Error z-value p-value low0.95CI.LP #> (Intercept) -2.38653694 0.97654087 -2.4438680 0.014530743 -4.30052187 #> M$age 0.04583409 0.01630956 2.8102598 0.004950153 0.01386795 #> M$sexM -0.87002367 0.45075104 -1.9301645 0.053586456 -1.75347948 #> M$hyperlipidemia 0.28922601 0.47408107 0.6100771 0.541810727 -0.63995581 #> high0.95CI.LP P_OR low0.95CI.P_OR high0.95CI.P_OR #> (Intercept) -0.47255201 0.0842051 0.01338003 0.3840124 #> M$age 0.07780024 1.0469007 1.01396455 1.0809067 #> M$sexM 0.01343214 0.4189416 0.17317035 1.0135228 #> M$hyperlipidemia 1.21840783 1.3353935 0.52731572 3.3817991 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} Age stays significant; sex is borderline; the comorbidity adjustment is not significant. On ~100 patients power is limited — the larger **GiBleed** study (next) delivers a strongly significant result. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} DSI::datashield.logout(conns) ``` ::: # Where to go next You have the full toolkit: **connect → explore → recipe (variables / format / filters / output, single or multiple) → execute → ratify → summarise → model**. Next: the **[exercise sheet](omop-exercises.html)**, then the larger **[GiBleed study](gibleed.html)**.
